segments.title: Opening: guitars, names, birthplace and age
segments.summary: Talk about Lewis's guitars, then everyone gives their names; Lewis was born in Greenwood, Mississippi, 6 March 1893, age 74.

segments.title: Coming to Memphis at 12-13; jug bands and big bands on Beale Street
segments.summary: Lewis was raised in Memphis; plenty of string band, jug band and larger band music then. He never played in the traveling big bands.

segments.title: W. C. Handy and the roadhouse called Pee Wee on Beale Street
segments.summary: Lewis knew Handy, who started at Pee Wee, a wide-open roadhouse on Beale Street where musicians hung out.

segments.title: Making a cigar-box guitar and teaching himself
segments.summary: Lewis began at 10 or 11 with a homemade cigar-box guitar and learned by ear with no teacher.

segments.title: Benevolent clubs and funeral marches before 1917
segments.summary: Social clubs had death benefits and bands marched at funerals playing hymns; the practice had mostly stopped by 1917, when Lewis lost his leg.

segments.title: After the funeral: all-night playing and where the band went
segments.summary: Bands played at the graveside, then went to someone's house to drink and play all night rather than return to the lodge hall.

segments.title: Listening to big bands; first job alone and the Chicago record
segments.summary: Lewis enjoyed big bands, his first music job was solo, and he made a record in Chicago on Wabash Street.

segments.title: Guitar tunings and Jack's offer of a guitar
segments.summary: Lewis tunes four ways (E, Spanish, Vestapol, cross note); Jack and Allen discuss checking pitches with a tuning fork and Jack offers a nylon-string guitar.

segments.title: Waiting on a first check; arranging the next visit
segments.summary: Lewis has not received his first check, and the others make plans for tomorrow and for dropping off a guitar; muddled ASR repeats parts.

segments.title: Singing before playing; Charlie Jackson and Landis Waldron
segments.summary: Lewis sang before he played, alongside guitarists Charlie Jackson and Landis Waldron, and picked up tuning by ear.

segments.title: Medicine show songs, leaving Greenwood, and country suppers
segments.summary: Lewis sang on a medicine show in Mississippi, Arkansas and Missouri and describes country suppers with dancing, food and whiskey.

segments.title: Corn whiskey talk
segments.summary: Lewis and Allen discuss corn whiskey, how good straight-from-the-still liquor differs from watered-down store stuff.

segments.title: The medicine show troupe and the two doctors
segments.summary: Lewis names his troupe (Willie Pope, Jim Jackson, Little Bob) and describes the two doctors, Richard Lewis and Dr. Fuller, selling medicine from a big van.

segments.title: Will Shade's last years and death
segments.summary: Lewis recalls Will Shade living nearby, sick for years, burned in a fall, and how Lewis and his wife brought him food.

segments.title: Never paid royalties on his 1959 records
segments.summary: Lewis got $400 for his 1959 record but no royalties, and Allen suggests finding a lawyer.

segments.title: Where is Memphis Minnie; Lewis's lack of income
segments.summary: They ask after Memphis Minnie, and Lewis says he still has no income coming in.

segments.title: Sleepy John Estes and directions to Booker White's house
segments.summary: Lewis recalls being in New York with Sleepy John and gives detailed directions to Booker White's home on Mosby Street.

segments.title: Joints with big bands, jug bands and guitar players
segments.summary: Allen asks about the kinds of bands in Memphis joints; Lewis names a few places, with ASR looping, and says there were many jug bands.

segments.title: Shade, Gus Cannon, and the other jug bands
segments.summary: Lewis was with Shade and traveled with Gus Cannon to New York, though not in the jug band; another band was led by a harmonica player called Ham.

segments.title: Naming old Memphis jug band musicians; Charlie Burse; why they left
segments.summary: Allen runs through names such as Noah Lewis, Hosey Woods and Charlie Burse; Lewis knows some, offers to call one, and says many left town.

segments.title: Theater bands, Johnny Dunn, Williamson and pianist Frenchie
segments.summary: Live music in theaters was rare; Allen asks about Johnny Dunn, Charlie Williamson's orchestra and pianist Frenchie.

segments.title: The Monarch joint, Winding Boy, and tape ending
segments.summary: Lewis describes the Monarch as a big rough joint with gambling; he does not know Winding Boy, and the tape runs out.
